GLOSSARY OF AERONAUTICAL AND ASTRONAUTICAL TERMS 

PART III STRUCTURE 



0, Foreword 

0.1 Provides standard definitions of technical terms peculiar to aeronautics, astronautics and related 
subjects. Terms In general use In other branches of engineering are also included where they have 
some special relevance to aeronautics or astronautics. 

0.2 This standard consists of a series of parts, each part covering terms specific 10 a particular feature, 
type of aircraft, equipment, service, etc. 

0.3 The general arrangement of the terms is alphabetical. However, in certain cases, related terms 
have been given together under a heading or general definition, and these are printed in distinctive 
italic type. 

0.4 Each term has been assigned a 4* dig it or 5-digit number. The first one (or two) digit, in the 
thousandth place, represents the part number. This part number with the following digit In the hundredth 
place represents the section. The last two digits represent the position of the definition within 
section. Thus the term 3405 is the 5th definition of Section 34, which is in Part 111. 

0.5 Where two or more synonymous terms are in uso f the term which la favoured is given first with 
the intention that it should gradually displace the others. The alternative terms are given below the 
preferred terms in less prominent type. 

0*6 An Indian Standard Glossary of space terms covering definitions pertaining to rockets* missiles, 
etc, is also under preparation. 

0.7 Assistance has been derived from BS 185 'Aeronautical and aeronautical terms' issued by the 
British Standards Institution, In the preparation of this series of Indian Standards. 



1. Scope — This part covers the standard definitions for terms relating to the structures of an aircraft. 

2, Terminology 

SECTION 31 — GENERAL 
No. Term Definition 

31 01 Buckling A structural deformation due initially to instability under load, 

irrespective of whether the deformation is elastic or 
permanent and whether it leads at once to collapse 
or not 

3102 Creep Buckling Critical terminal buckling resulting from stow and steady 

increase in the deformation of a structure under a 
constant load. 

3103 Thermal Buckling Buckling induced wholly or in part by thermal stressor by 

thermal distortion. 

31 04 Factor of Safety The factor by which a limit toad is multiplied to produce the 

load to be used in the design of en aircraft or pan of 
an aircraft. It la introduced to provide a margin of 
strength against loads greater than the limit loads, and 
against uncertainties In materials* construction, load 
estimation and stress analysis. 

3105 Proof factor The factor of safety corresponding to the proof load.

31 20 Primary Structure 



Definition 

The factor of safety corresponding to the load which is 
regarded ss the ultimate for design purposes, that is, 
the fully-factorsd load. 

The ratio of the length of a body to its maximum transverse 
dimension or, sometimes, to some equivalent dimension. 

Flexural centre of a cross-section is defined as a point In 
that section at which a shear force can be applied 
without producing a rotation of that section in its own 

plane. 

A diagram in which, for a particular aircraft type, the 
specified design normal accelerations (as multiples of g) 
form the ordtnates and the corresponding equivalent air- 
speeds the abscissae. The boundary of the diagram 
forms a closed figure which defines the design limits 
for the aircraft concerned. 

The maximum toad which a structure Is required to be 
capable of withstanding. 

A method of making curved space frames in which the 
principal structural members follow geodesies in the 
surface, so that the forces set up in the members are 
either tensile or compressive. 

A correction factor which allows for gust shape, aircraft 
flexibility, freedom in pitch and delay in the giowin of 
the lift increment. The factor is applied to the increment 
in acceleration found from a simple calculation of the 
response to a sharp-edged gust in which no allowance 
Is made for these effects. 

A diagram In which, for a particular aircraft type, the gust 
load factors form the ordinates and the corresponding 
equivalent airspeeds the abscissae, and on which 
contours of constant vertical gust velocity can be drawn. 
It Is often superimposed on the flight envelope because 
of the common abscissae. 

The number of discrete gusts encountered per unit horizontal 
distance ( usually one mile ) having vertical velocity 
equal to or greater than a given value- 

The formation of a structural member as a single whole 
instead of by the assembly of a large number of separate 
elements. 

The maximum load expected to be applied, in a particular 
condition of operation, to the aircraft or to any part 
of it. 

The process by which variation along any length of a structure 
of transverse distribution of stress, due to direct loads 
applied in the direction of that length, is established. 

The type of load diffusion in which the lag of longitudinal 
displacement of one part of a transverse section relative 
to that of another results primarily from shear loading 
applied along lines parallel to the length of the 
structure. 

The ratio of the total load in a specified direction ( usually 
along the normal axis ) to the weight of the aircraft. 
Such load may arise from the aerodynamic forces, 
gravity, ground or water reaction, or from combinations 
of these forces. 

Those portions of the structure the failure of which would 
seriously endanger the aircraft in flight.

3131 Ultimate Load 



Definition 

The load which a structure is required to withstand and trill 

remain serviceable. 

The ratio of the ultimate load of a structure to the fully- 
factored load. 

A hypothetical discrete vertical ( or side ) gust fn which the 
velocity of the air changes abruptly, that is, the gutl 
gradient distance is zero. 

A device, embodying a sensing element attached 10 the 
structure, which provides a direct measurement of strain 
at the point of attachment. 

A set of strain gauges at a point on the surface of e structure, 
so arranged that the state of plane strain at the point can 
be fully determined. 

A common form of strain gauge in which the sensing 
element comprises one or more lengths of fine wire, the 
change In whose electrical resistance under load pro- 
vides a measure of the strain. 

A structure covered with sheet which contributes substantially 
to its strength and stiffness. 

A stress induced when a structure embodying materials with 
different coefficients of linear expansion is exposed to a 
temperature other than that prevailing at the time of 
assembly. 

An apparatus far subjecting aircraft structures to loads 
representing those occurring in operation, ft comprises 
loading and supporting frameworks and a control 
mechanism for the application of loads by hydraulic Jacks 
or other means. 

The stress induced within a structure by changes In tempe- 
rature.

SECTION 32— DETAIL PARTS 

A streamlined protuberance on an aircraft, designed to house 
equipment, to afford a place for observation or for other 

purposes. 

The rear portion of an elongated body, as a rocket, having 
cross- sectional area decreasing toward the rear. 

A transverse dividing wall within a structure. 

The extreme side member of the planing bottom running 
approximately paraffel to the keel in side elevation. 

Describes doors or other structural parts which open and 
close in the manner of clamshells, 

A quick- opening cockpit window ( panel ) allowing direct 
vision. 

A quick release device actuated by a small explosive charge 
detonated by an electneel or other signal. 

A secondary structure added to any part to reduce its 
drag. 

A fairing at the junction of two surfaces to Improve the 
airflow*

Definition 

The principal structural member of a fin, usually carrying the 
rudder. 

A structural mem ben the primary purpose of which is to pre- 
serve form or shape and to which the external skin is 
attached* in general, it carries structural loads. 

o) Generally, a plane structure transverse to the axis of a 
tube and maintaining the shape of the cross section of 
ths tubs. 

b) Specifically, a structural member lying in a transverse 
plana of a fuselage, hull or nacelle, and following the 
periphery- 

A specialty strong frame in the plane of any spar. 

A longitudinal member forming part of the main structure 
of a hull or float and running internally along trie 
bottom. 

A main longitudinal member of a fuselage or nacelle- 

A type of structure whose strength end rigidity depends upon 
the outer surface, usually with strong circumferential 
members. 

A portion of a stiffened sheet together with its siiffeners. 

a) In structural theory, a portion of an unstiffened sheet 

b) A sheet having thickness greater than a specified amount. 

A member which maintains the required contour of the 
covering material of planes or control surfaces, end 
which may also act as a structural member. 

A former between the front spar and leading edge of an 
aerofoil. 

The principal structural member of a rudder, usually carrying 
the hinges (see 3231). 

A structural component consisting of two parallel, or nearly 
parallel, faces attached to either side of a core of 
material of different properties. 

The material between the faces of a sandwich. \\ stabilizes 
them and may carry direct load. 

A sandwich In which the core is built up from sheet having 
longitudinal corrugations, enabling it to carry direct 
load in the longitudinal direction. 

The external skins of a sandwich. 

A sandwich En which the cord is formed of thin-wailed small 
celts, often, but not necessarily, hexagonal in shape. 
It is usual to assume that the core will carry negligible 
direct toad parallel to the faces. 

Material of which the thickness is small in comparison with 
the other dimensions. 

A curved structure formed of sheet (either stiffened or 
unstiffened) generally closed on itself as in a tube. 

Sheet covering a framework of stiffeners. 

A principal spanwise structural member of an aerofoil or 
control surface. 

A single member terminating a fuselage, hull or float 
(see 3221).

3310 Flutter 



IS: 7879 (Pert lit )-(t75 

Definition 

A member attached to a sheet to restrain its movement 
norma* to the surface. 

A stiffener which also assists the sheet to carry direct toad 
In the direction of its length. 

A structural member intended to resist compression. 

Struts incorporated In the framework of an aerofoil to carry 
the loads induced by the air forces in the plane of the 
aerofoil. 

Struts connecting a plane to the plane above or below. 

Wires or cables incorporated In the framework of an aerofoil 
and in its plane, complementary to the drag wires and 
resisting forces in the opposite direction. 

Wires to resist forces In the opposite direction to the lift. 



Wires or cables incorporated in the framework of an aerofoil 
and in its plane, to resist forces in the general direction 
of the drag, 

Wires or cables bracing the main plane structure in the 
plane of a pair of front and rear struts. 

Wires or cables the principal function of which ia to transfer 
the lift of the main planes to the main structure, 

A wire the cross section of which is elongated to reduce its 
drag. 

SECTION 33— AEftOELASTICITY 

The fteroelastic instability which results when the rate of 
change of aerodynamic forces or couples with displace- 
ment exceeds that of the elastic restoring forces or 
couples. 

The lowest equivalent air speed at which aeroelastic 
divergence occurs. 

A branch of mechanics which treats of the phenomena 
resulting from the Interaction of aerodynamic, inertia! 
and elastic forces. 

That branch of aeroelastic rty in which aerodynamic heating 
of the structure is considered* 

An oscillation, of limited empfitude, of a control surface 
about its hinge. tt can occur at high subsonic and 
transonic speeds. 

An irregular oscillation of any part of an aircraft produced 
and maintained directly by an eddying flow. 



The damping intrinsic to the material of the structure* 
The total damping of a built-up structure. 

A flight test during which the structure of an aircraft is 
excited in order to observe its behaviour and to deduce 
its flutter characteristics. 

A sustained oscillation due to the interaction between aero- 
dynamic forces, elastic reactions and Inertia.

Definition 

Flutter in which the components on port and starboard sides 
of an aircraft undergo, at any instant, equal but asymmet- 
rical displacement with respect to the plane of symmetry. 

Flutter in which the components on the port and starboard 
aides of an aircraft undergo, at any instant, asymmetrical 
and unequal displacements with respect to the plane of 
symmetry. 

Flutter which occurs because of coupling (inertiaf, aero- 
dynamic or elastic) between two or more degrees of 
freedom* 

The lowest equivalent airspeed at which flutter occurs. 

Flutter in one or more degrees of freedom around the angle 
of stall. 

Flutter in which the components on the port and starboard 
sides of an aircraft undergo, at any instant, equal and 
symmetrical displacements with respect to the plane of 
symmetry. 

The ratio of the product of the frequency of an oscillation and 
a representative length of en oscillating system to the 
true airspeed. 

A mass normally attached to a control surface forward of the 
hinge line, for the purpose of reducing or eliminating 
the ineriial coupling between angular movement of the 
control and some other degree of fieedom of the aircraft. 

A mass-balance weight which is distributed along the span 
of the control surface. 

A mass- balance weight which is connected to the control 
surface by a series of finks. 

A mode of free vibration of an undamped system. 

A section of a structure, the displacements of which are 
taken as the co-ordinates in a semi-rigid representation. 

A test in which forced oscillation over a range of frequencies 
is applied to a structure with the object of determining 
the natural frequencies and modes of oscillation of the 
structure. 

The condition in which the displacement of a control surface 
produces a moment on the aircraft in a reverse Sense 
because of excessive structural distortion. 

The lowest equivalent airspeed at which reversal of control 
occurs. 

An approximate theory of elastic structures In which the 
theoretical infirtiw number of degrees of freedom is 
represented by a finite number, each being associated 
with an invariable mode. 

The condition of a control surface in which the mass- 
balance is such that the centre of mass lies on the 
hinge axis. 

A relationship between the stiffness and other properties 
of a structure which, when satisfied, is sufficient to 
prevent flutter or other type of instability or loss of 
control. 

That part of the effective inertia £ mass ) of an oscillating 
body which is due to the presence of the surrounding air 
and Is proportional to the density of that air.

Fatigue due to repeated loading produced by sound waves. 

A test in which a specimen is subjected to acoustic loading 
In a test channel or reverberant chamber, or in the open. 

A test in which the specimen is subjected to sound waves 
off only one frequency. 

A test in which the specimen is subjected simultaneously Co 
sound waves covering a broad band of frequencies. 

The number of stress cycles to failure at a constant amplitude 
and constant mean stress, preferably given as a fraction 
or multiple of 10* cycles. In programme loading, 
endurance may be expressed aa the number of prog- 
rammes to failure, 

A structure which retains, after the Initiation of a fracture 
or crack, sufficient strength and stiffness for the operation 
of the aircraft with an acceptable standard of safety 
until such fracture or crack is detected by normal inspec- 
tion procedure. 

The operational life of an aircraft or component expressed as 
a number of flying hours or flights or of applications of 
load during which the general level of structural safety 
is not appreciably lowered by fatigue. 

The highest level of alternating stress for a given mean 
stress at which the endurance Is infinite. 

The alternating stress at a specified mean stress which causes 
failure at a given number of cycles. 

The ratio of the fatigue strength of a plain specimen to that 
of a similar specimen with a stress concentration, under 
the same external loads. 

A water tank, with the necessary ancillary equipment, in 
which a scaled body (for example, the pressure cabin of 
an aircraft > is wholly immersed and subjected to cyclic 
variations of internal water pressure. Provision may also 
be made for the simultaneous imposition of cyclic load- 
ing to the remainder of the aircraft. 



A load cycle In which the load does not change sign. 
usually with zero minimum load. 

A load cycle with zero mean load. 

That which arises solely from the shape of the part, as derived 
from elastic theory or from strain measurements during 
which the material remains elastic throughout 

The average of the algebraic values of the maximum and 
minimum loads of the fatigue loading cycle. 

The excursion from the mean load. 

The difference between maximum and minimum loads. 

The ratio of the minimum to the maximum load.

A set of predetermined loads, applied repeatedly, each time 
Jn random order until f ai Jure or for the required number

A diagram In which the logarithm of endurance is plotted,

Fatigue produced by fluctuations of temperature. 

In acoustics, pertaining to frequencies above those detect*

Indian Standard ( Reaffirmed 2005 ) 
GLOSSARY OF AERONAUTICAL AND ASTRON AUTICAL TERMS 

PART III STRUCTURE 



0. Foreword 

0,1 Provides standard definitions of technical terms peculiar to aeronautics, astronautics and related 
subjects. Terms in general use in other branches of engineering ate also included where they two 
some special relevance to aeronautics or astronautics. 

0.2 This standard consists of a series of parts, each part covering terms specific to a particular feature, 
type of aircraft, equipment, service, etc. 

0.3 The general arrangement of the terms is alphabetical. However, in certain cases, related terms 
" have been given together under a heading or general definition, and these are printed in distinctive 
* italic type. 



0.4 Each term has been assigned a 4-diglt or 5- digit number. The first one (or two) digit, in the 
thousandth place, represents the pan number. This part number with the following digit in the hundredth 
place represents the section. The lest two digits represent the position of the definition within a 
section. Thus the term 3405 [s the 5th definitLon of Section 34, which is in Part III. 

0.5 Where two or more synonymous terms are in use, the term which is favoured is given first, with 
the intention that it should gradually displace the others. The alternative terms are given below the 
preferred terms in less prominent type. 

0.0 An Indian Standard Glossary of space terms coverfng definitions pertaining to rockets, missiles. 
etc, is also under preparation. 

0.7 Assistance has been derived from 63 186 ' Aeronautical and astronautics! terms' issued by the 
British Standards Institution, in the preparation of this series of Indian Standards. 



1. Scope — This part covers the standard definitions for terms relating to the structure* of an aircraft. 
2* Terminology 

SECTION 31 — GENERAL 
No. Term Definition 

31 01 Buckling A structural deformation due initially to instability under load, 

irrespective of whether the deformation is elastic or 
permanent and whether it leads at once to collapse 
or not. 

3102 Creep Buckling Critical terminal buckling resulting from slow and steady 

increase in the deformation of a structure under a 
constant load. 

3103 Thermal Buckling Buckling induced wholly or in part by thermal stressor by 

thermal distortion. 

3104 Factor of Safety The facto? by which a limit load vs multiplied to produce the 

load to be used in the design of en aircraft or pan of 
an aircraft, ft is introduced to provide a margin of 
strength against loads greater than the limit loads, and 
against uncertainties in materials, construction, foad 
estimation and swesa analysis. 

31 05 Proof Factor The factor of safety corresponding to the proof load.

31 1 9 Load Factor 



3120 Primary Structure 



Definition 

The factor of safety corresponding to the load which is 
regarded as the ultimate for design purposes, that is, 
the fully-factored load. 

The ratio of the length of a body to its maximum transversa 
dimsnslon or, sometimes, to some equivalent dimension. 

Flexure I centre of a cross -section is defined as a point in 
that section at which a shear force can be applied 
without producing a rotation of that section in its own 
plane. 

A diagram in which, for a particular aircraft type, the 
specified design normal accelerations (as multiples of g) 
form the ordinates and the corresponding equivalent air- 
speeds the abscissae, ThB boundary of the diagram 
forms a closed figure which defines tha design limits 
for the aircraft concerned. 

The maximum load which a structure is required to be 
capable of withstanding. 

A method of making curved space frames in which the 
principal structural members follow geodesies in the 
su rface, so that the forces set up in the members are 
either tensile or compressive* 

A correction factor which allows for Oust shape, aircraft 
flexibility, freedom in pitch and delay in the growth of 
the lift increment. The factor is applied to the increment 
in acceleration found from a simple calculation of the 
response to a sharp-edged gust in which no allowance 
is made for these effects. 

A diagram fn which, for a particular aircraft type, the gust 
load factors form the ordinates and the corresponding 
equivalent airspeeds the abscissae, and on which 
contours of constant vertical gust velocity can be drawn. 
It is often superimposed on the flight envelope because 
of the common abscissae. 

The number of discrete gusts encountered per unit horizontal 
distance (usually one mile ) having vertical veJocity 
equal to or greater than a given value. 

The formation of a structural member as a single whole 
instead of by the assembly of a large number of separate 
elements. 

The maximum load expected to be applied, in a particular 
condition of operation, to the aircraft or to any part 
Of It. 

The process by which variation along any length of a structure 
of transverse distribution of stress, due to direct loads 
applied in the direction of that length, is established. 

The type of load diffusion in which the lag of longitudinal 
displacement of one part of a transverse section relative 
to that of another results primarily from shear loading 
applied along tines parallel to the lengih of the 
structure. 

The ratio of the total load in a specified direction ( usually 
along the normal axis ) to the weight of the aircraft. 
Such load may arise from the aerodynamic forces, 
gravity, ground or water reaction, or from combinations 
of these forces. 

Those portions of the structure the failure of which would 
seriously endanger the aircraft in flight

3131 Ultimate Load 



Definition 

The load which a structure h required to withstand and still 
remain serviceable. 

The ratio of the ultimate load of a structure to the fully- 
factored load, 

A hypothetical discrete vertical ( or side ) gust In which the 
velocity of the air changes abruptly, that is, the gust 
gradient distance is zero. 

A device, embodying a sensing element attached to the 
structure, which provides a direct measurement of strain 
at the point of attachment. 

A set of strain gauges at a point on the surface of a structure, 
so arranged that the state of plane strain at the point can 
be fully determined. 

A common form of strain gauge in which the sensing 
element comprises one or more lengths of fine wire, the 
change In whose electrical resistance under load pro- 
vides a measure or the strain. 

A structure covered with sheet which contributes substantially 
to its suengm and stiffness. 

A stress induced when a structure embodying materials with 
different coefficients of linear expansion is exposed to a 
temperature other then that prevailing at the time of 
assembly. 

An apparatus for subjecting aircraft structures to toads 
representing those occurring in operation. It comprises 
loading and supporting frameworks and a control 
mechanism for the application of loads by hydraulic facks 
or other means. 

The stress induced within a structure by changes in tempe- 
rature.

SECTION 32— DETAIL PARTS 

A streamlined protuberance on an aircraft, designed to house 
equipment, to afford a place for observation or for other 

purposes. 

The rear portion of an elongated body, as a rocket, having 
cross-sectional area decreasing toward the rear. 

A transverse dividing wall within a structure. 

The extreme side member of the planing bottom running 
approximately parallel to the keel in side elevation. 

Describes doors or other structural parts which open and 
close in the manner of clamshells. 

A quick-opening cockpit window ( panel ) allowing direct 
vision. 

A quick release device actuated by a small explosive charge 
detonated by an electrical or other signal. 

A secondary structure added to any part to reduce its 
drag. 

A fairing at the junction of two surfaces to Improve the 
airflow.

3231 Stern Post 



Definition 

The principal structural member of a fin, usually carrying the 
rudder. 

A structural member, the primary purpose of which is to pre- 
serve form or shape and to which the external skin is 
attached. In general, it carries structural loads. 

a) Generally, a plane structure transversa to the axis of a 

tube and maintaining the shape of the cross section of 
the tube. 

b) Specifically, a structural member lying in a transverse 

plane of a fuselage, hull or nacelle, and following the 
periphery. 

A specially strong frame in the plane of any spar. 

A longitudinal member forming part of the main structure 
of a hull or float and running internally along the 
bottom. 

A main longitudinal member of a fuselage or nacelle. 

A type of structure whose strength and rigidity depends upon 
the outer surface, usually with strong circumferential 
members . 

A portion of a stilfened sheet together with its stiffeners. 

a) !n structural theory, a portion of an unsti ff en &d sheet, 

b) A sheet having thickness greater than a specified amount. 

A member which maintains the required contour of the 
covering material of planes or control surfaces, and 
which may also act as a structural member. 

A former between the front spar and leading edge of an 
aerofoil. 

The principal structural member of a rudder, usually carrying 
the hinges (see 3231). 

A structural component consisting of two parallel, or nearly 
parallel, faces attached to either side of a core of 
material of different properties. 

The material between the faces of a sandwich, ft stabilizes 
them and may carry direct load. 

A sandwich In which the core is built up from sheet having 
longitudinal corrugations, enabling it to carry direct 
toed in the longitudinal direction. 

The external skins of a sandwich. 

A sandwich En which the core is formed of thin-walled small 
cells, often, but not necessarily, hexagonal in shape. 
It is usual to assume that the core will carry negligible 
direct load parallel to the feces. 

Material of which the thickness is small in comparison with 
the other dimensions. 

A curved structure formed of sheet (either stiffened or 
un stiffened) generally closed on itself as in a tube. 

Sheet covering a framework of stiffeners. 

A principal spanwise structural member of an aerofoil or 
control surface. 

A single member terminating a fuselage, hull or float 
(see 3221).

3310 Flutter 



IS: 787? (Part III)- 1*75 

Definition 

A member attached to a sheet to restrain its movement 
normal to the surface. 

A stiffener which also assists the sheet to cairv direct load 
in the direction of its length. 

A structural member intended to resist compression, 

Struts incorporated in the framework of an aerofoil to carry 
the loads induced by the air forces in the plane of the 
aerofoil. 

Struts connecting a plane to the plane above or below. 

Wires or cables incorporated in the framework of an aerofoil 
and in its plane, complementary to the drag wires and 
resisting forces in the opposite direction. 

Wires to resist forces in the opposite direction to the lift. 

Wires or cables incorporated in the framework of an aerofoil 
and in its plane, to resist farces in the general direction 
of the drag. 

Wires or cables bracing the main plane structure in the 
plane of a pair of front and rear struts. 

Wires or cables the principal function of which Is to transfer 
the lift of the main planes to the main structure. 

A wire the cross section of which is elongated to reduce its 
drag. 

SECTION 33— AEROELASTIClTY 

The aeroelastic instability which results when the rate of 
change of aerodynamic forces or couples with displace- 
ment exceeds that of the elastic restoring forces or 
couples. 

The lowest equivalent air speed at which aeroefastic 
divergence occurs. 

A branch of mechanics which treats of trie phenomena 
resulting from the interaction of aerodynamic, inertial 
and elastic forcee. 

That branch of aeroelasticity in which aerodynamic heating 
of the structure is considered. 

An oscillation, of limited amplitude, of a control surface 
about its hinge. It can occur at high subsonic and 
transonic speeds. 

An irregular oscillation of any part of an aircraft produced 
and maintained directly by an eddying flow. 



The damping intrinsic to the material of the structure. 
The total damping of a built-up structure. 

A flight test during which the structure of an aircraft Is 
excited in order to observe its behaviour and to deduce 
its flutter characteristics. 

A sustained oscillation due to the interaction between aero- 
dynamic Iqrces, elastic reactions and Inertia.

3329 Virtual Inertia ( Mass ) 



Definition 

Flutter in which the components on port end starboard sides 
of an aircraft undergo, at any instant, equal but asymmet- 
rical displacement with respect to the plane of symmetry. 

Flutter in which the components on the port and starboard 
sides of an aircraft undergo, at any instant, asymmetrical 
and unequal displacements with respect to the plane of 
symmetry. 

Flutter which occurs because of coupling (inertial, aero- 
dynamic or elastic) between two or more degrees of 
freedom. 

The lowest equivalent airspeed at which flutter occurs. 

Flutter In one or more degrees of freedom around the angle 
of stall. 

Flutter In which the components on the port and starboard 
sides of an aircraft undergo, at any instant, equal and 
symmetrical displacements wtth respect to the plane of 
symmetry. 

The ratio of the product of the frequency of an oscillation and 
a representative length of an oscillating system to the 
true airspeed. 

A mass normally attached to a control surface forward of the 
hinge line, for the purpose of reducing or eliminating 
the inenial coupling between angular movement of the 
control and some other degree of freedom of the aircraft. 

A mass-balance weight which is distributed along the span 
of the control surface. 

A mass-balance weight which is connected to the control 
surface by a series of links. 

A mode of free vibration of an undamped system. 

A section of a structure, the displacements of which are 
taken as the co-ordinates in a semi-rigid representation, 

A test in which forced oscillation over a range of frequencies 
Is applied to a structure with ihe object of determining 
the natural frequencies and modes of oscillation of the 
structure. 

The condition in which the displacement of a control surface 
produces a moment on the aircraft in a reverse sense 
because of excessive structural distortion, 

The lowest equivalent airspeed at which reversal of control 
occurs. 

An approximate theory of elastic structures in which the 
theoretical infinite number of degrees of freedom is 
represented by a finite number, each being associated 
with an invariable mode. 

The condition of a control surface In which the mass- 
balance Is such that the centre of mass lies on the 
hinge axis. 

A relationship between the stiffness and other properties 
of a structure which, when satisfied, is sufficient to 
prevent flutter or other type of instability or loss of 
control. 

That part of the effective inertia { mass ) of an oscillating 
body which is due to the presence of the surrounding air 
and is proportional to the density of that air

SECTION 34 — FATIGUE 



Definition 

Fatigue due to repeated loading produced by sound waves. 

A test In which a specimen is subjected to acoustic loading 
in a test channel or reverberant chamber, or in the open. 

A test in which the specimen Is subjected to sound waves 
of only one frequency. 

A test In which the specimen is subjected simultaneously to 
sound waves covering a broad band of frequencies. 

The number of stress cycles to failure at a constant amplitude 
and constant mean stress, preferably given as a fraction 
or multiple of 10* cycles. In programme loading, 
endurance may be expressed as the number of prog- 
rammes to failure. 

A structure which retains, after the initiation of a fracture 
or crack, sufficient strength and stiffness for the operation 
of the aircraft with an acceptable standard of safety 
until such fracture or crack is detected by normal inspec- 
tion procedure. 

The operational life of en aircraft or component, expressed as 
a number of flying hours or flights or of applications of 
load during which the general level of structural safety 
is not appreciably lowered by fatigue. 

The highest level of alternating stress for a given mean 
stress at which the endurance is infinite. 

The alternating stress at a specified mean stress which causes 
failure at a given number of cycles. 

The ratio of the fatigue strength of a plain specimen to that 
of a similar specimen with a stress concentration, under 
the same external loads. 

A water tank, with the necessary ancillary equipment, in 
which a scaled body (for example,- the pressure cabin of 
an aircraft ) is wholly immersed and subjected to cyclic 
variations of internal water pressure. Provision may also 
be made for the simultaneous imposition of cyclic load* 
ing to the remainder of the aircraft. 



A load cycle in which the load does not change sign* 
usually with zero minimum load. 

A load cycle with zero mean load. 

That which arises solely from the shape of the part, as derived 
from elastic theory or from strain measurements during 
which the material remains elastic throughout. 



The average of the algebraic values of the maximum and 
minimum loads of the fatigue loading cycle. 

The excursion from the mean load. 

The difference between maximum and minimum loads. 

The ratio of the minimum to the maximum load*

Definition 

The region In the vicinity of a noise source in which the 
fluid particle velocity >a not necessarily rn the direction 
of travel of the wave, end an appreciable tangential 
velocity may exist at any point, in this region the 
acoustic intensity Is not simply related to the sound 
pressure squared. 

A set of predetermined loads, applied in a definite order 
and repeated until failure Or for a specified number of 
times. 

A random sequence of loads defined by a continuous 
spectrum of known statistical properties. 

A set of predetermined loads, applied repeatedly, eac h time 
in random order until failure or for the required number 
of times. 

A disQtem in which the logarithm of endurance is plotted, 
as abscissa, against the alternating stress (semi- log 
plot) or Its logarithm (log -log plot), as ordinate. 

That fife during which the probability of fatigue failure is 
below a specified low levef. 

A diagram in which contours of constant endurance are 
plotted with alternating stress as ordinate and mean 
stress es abscissa. 

A phenomenon which may occur in the efflux of a jet engine 
with certain nozzle configurations and supBT-critical 
pressure ratios. It can give rise to high sound intensities 
contained within a relatively small bandwidth. 

The mean square value of the quantity in a band one cycle 
per second wide, centred at a specified frequency. 

Sinusoidal loading of constant spectral density over a band- 
width appreciably less than one octave. 

Sinusoidal loading of constant spectral density over a band- 
width greater than one octave. 

The ratio of the highest strain to a reference strain calculable 
from simple theory. 

A local increase in the Intensity of a stress field in a region 
surrounding a discontinuity. The discontinuity may be 
one of shape (for example, hole, notch, crack, surface 
defect), metallurgical origin (for example, inclusion) or 
local distribution of load (for example, pin-joint). 

The ratio of the highest stress to a reference stress calcul- 
able from simple theory. 

The average of the algebraic values of the maximum and 
minimum stresses of the fatigue loading cycle. 

The excursion from the mean stress. 

The difference between maximum and minimum stresses. 

The ratio of the minimum to the maximum stress. 

Fatigue produced by fluctuations of temperature- 

In acoustics, pertaining to frequencies above those detect- 
able by the human ear, often taken as higher than 
20 000 vibrations per second.
